The SWIFT multiblock Navier-Stokes analysis code was used for the turbomachinery simulations.
Giles' characteristic boundary conditions were used at the averaging planes to allow close spacing between blade rows without forcing the flow to be axisymmetric.
Two averaging techniques were used: the mixed-out average and the kinetic energy average.
The two-stage fuel turbine from the space shuttle main engine was analyzed, with a total grid size of about 1.09 million points.
The computed mass flow rate of 2.644 kg/sec (5.83 lb/sec) matched the experimental measurement exactly.
The computed surface pressure distributions and blade heat transfer coefficients showed very good agreement with experimental data.
Eigenvalue scaling and preconditioning were used to improve the numerical convergence of the low-Mach number flow.
The mixed-out average represents the flow after mixing losses, while the kinetic energy average represents the local state of the flow.
The characteristic boundary conditions produced a much smoother pressure field near the exit compared to a constant-pressure condition in the two-dimensional analysis.
The averaging-plane method maintains spanwise consistency between blade rows but still has some modeling limitations compared to full unsteady methods.
The average-passage method provides a rigorous foundation for modeling unsteady blade row interaction but has not been widely used due to its complexity.
Successive analysis of isolated blade rows is a simple approach but has many modeling issues, such as difficulty matching inlet and exit conditions between blade rows.
Full unsteady methods avoid many modeling assumptions but are computationally very expensive.
The SWIFT code uses an explicit finite-difference scheme with viscous terms in the blade-to-blade and hub-to-tip directions.
The Cebeci-Smith turbulence model was used, with all boundary layers assumed to be fully turbulent.
